Treat the problem as a statically determinate, small-deformation, linear-elastic torsion problem.
The body is a solid circular shaft of diameter d = 30 mm and total length L = 1200 mm.
The shaft is made of AISI 1020 steel with shear modulus G = 76,923.1 MPa.
Use a consistent unit system of N, mm, and MPa throughout the analysis.
The shaft is built-in (fixed) at x = 0 and free at x = L = 1200 mm.
Apply a torque T₁ = +200,000 N·mm at x = L = 1200 mm.
Apply a torque T₂ = −200,000 N·mm at x = 400 mm.
Take the sign convention such that positive torque follows the right-hand rule about the shaft axis (+x).
Compute the reactive torque at the fixed end x = 0 from moment equilibrium about the shaft axis.
Identify two segments for the internal torque distribution: segment 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 400 mm and segment 2 for 400 mm ≤ x ≤ 1200 mm.
Use the method of sections to derive the internal torque T(x) in each segment by summing external torques on either side of the cut.
Report the internal torque values T₁ (segment 1) and T₂ (segment 2) as piecewise-constant values between the applied torques.
Verify that the internal torque diagram satisfies jump discontinuities equal to the magnitude of each applied torque at x = 400 mm and x = 1200 mm.
Compute the polar moment of inertia of the solid circular cross section as J = π d⁴ / 32.
Use the linear-elastic torsion constitutive relation φ_i = T_i L_i / (J G) for the angle of twist in each segment.
Accumulate the segment-by-segment angles of twist, starting from the fixed end where θ(0) = 0.
Report the angle of twist θ(x) at x = 400 mm, x = 1200 mm, and specifically at the location of each applied torque.
Report the maximum angle of twist θ_max at the free end x = L.
Compute the shear stress distribution across the cross section in each segment as τ(r) = T r / J.
Evaluate the maximum shear stress τ_max at the outer surface r = d/2 in each segment and identify the governing segment.
Present all governing relations clearly: moment equilibrium ΣT = 0, kinematic relation dθ/dx = T/(JG), constitutive law τ_max = T r/J, and the angle-of-twist formula φ = TL/(JG).
Validate the solution by confirming θ(0) = 0 at the built-in end and that the net applied torque equals the reaction at x = 0.
State explicitly any additional assumptions used, including neglecting stress concentrations at torque application points, uniform G, and small deformations that permit superposition and linear elastic behavior.
